title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 07–08 (editorial revision)
description: Units 07–08 reviewed against the source teaching pages and exercises. Topics include feelings, preferences, hopes and wants, everyday greetings, wishes and congratulations. All instructional content and metadata are in English; Portuguese is restricted to pt translations.
sourceNotice: The supplied source was consulted to verify learning targets and coverage. Example sentences and explanatory notes are original. The package does not reproduce textbook illustrations, exercise pages or recordings.

audit.scope: Teaching sections A–D and exercises 7.1–7.5 plus Over to you for Unit 07; sections A–B and exercises 8.1–8.5 for Unit 08. Printed page layouts and exercise contexts were inspected.

units.title: Unit 07 — Feelings
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 7, printed pages 20–21 (PDF pages 21–22); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish love, like, do not like and hate on a preference scale, and use like followed by an -ing form.
Identify and describe emotions and physical sensations using be and feel with adjectives.
Use happy about for news or events and happy for a person who has had good news.
Compare preferences using prefer A to B and like A more than B.
Express wants and hopes using want + noun, want to + verb, want + person + to + verb, hope to and hope (that).
Place really and very much naturally with like, and avoid errors such as I very like.
Answer personal questions about feelings and correct common mistakes using a bit, a little and related expressions.

items.example: My grandparents love spending time together.
items.note: Love expresses a stronger positive feeling than like. It can be followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: I like listening to jazz in the evening.
items.note: Use like with a noun or an -ing form when talking about preferences: like music; like reading.

items.example: I don't like travelling on crowded trains.
items.note: Don't like expresses a negative preference, usually less strongly than hate.

items.example: My brother hates waiting in long queues.
items.note: Hate is stronger than don't like; use it with care when talking about people.

items.example: We were happy when the results arrived.
items.note: Happy describes a positive feeling. Compare happy about an event with happy for a person.

items.example: She felt sad after saying goodbye to her friends.
items.note: Sad describes unhappiness and can follow be or feel.

items.example: He was angry because the bus was late.
items.note: Angry means feeling annoyed or cross. Do not confuse it with hungry, meaning needing food.

items.example: I was upset when I heard the bad news.
items.note: Upset can describe unhappiness, worry or emotional distress; it is less specific than angry.

items.example: I'm cold. Could you close the window?
items.note: I'm cold describes how someone feels about the temperature. It does not necessarily mean the person is unfriendly.

items.example: I'm hot after that long walk.
items.note: I'm hot can describe feeling too warm; hot can also describe the temperature of a place or object.

items.example: I'm thirsty after the long walk.
items.note: Use I'm thirsty when you want something to drink; I have thirst is not natural in everyday conversation.

items.example: We were hungry after the swimming lesson.
items.note: Hungry describes wanting food. Notice the initial /h/ and the /ŋɡ/ consonant sequence.

items.example: My uncle is well again after a week of rest.
items.note: Well can be an adjective describing good health. In this context, compare well with ill.

items.example: The children felt ill during the trip.
items.note: Ill describes poor health. In British English, be ill and feel ill are common expressions.

items.example: The team was tired after the match.
items.note: Use be or feel with tired. In British English, this word may be pronounced with one or two syllables.

items.example: I was surprised to see my old teacher at the station.
items.note: Surprised describes the feeling caused by something unexpected. The final consonant group is /zd/.

items.example: We're happy about the new timetable.
items.note: Use happy about with news, an event or a situation, rather than with the person who benefits.

items.example: I'm happy for Mina because she passed her driving test.
items.note: Use happy for with a person who has experienced something good: happy for you.

items.example: I prefer cycling when the weather is good.
items.note: Prefer is used to choose one thing over another. A common pattern is prefer A to B.

items.example: I prefer walking to driving in the city centre.
items.note: Compare two options with prefer A to B. The dots represent variable phrases and should not be spoken aloud.

items.pt: gostar mais de uma coisa do que de outra
items.example: My sister likes tennis more than football.
items.note: Compare preferences with like A more than B. The dots stand for the things being compared.

items.example: I hope the weather improves tomorrow.
items.note: Hope expresses a wish or expectation that something will happen. Compare hope with want.

items.example: I hope to finish the course this year.
items.note: Use hope to followed by the base form of a verb when the same person hopes to do the action.

items.example: We hope that the train arrives on time.
items.note: Hope can introduce a clause with its own subject and verb. That is optional in many sentences.

items.example: I want a quiet room for the meeting.
items.note: Use want with a noun to say what someone wishes to have or get.

items.example: I want to practise English tonight.
items.note: Use want to followed by a base-form verb: want to leave; do not omit to.

items.example: My parents want me to call them this evening.
items.note: Use want + person + to + verb: I want you to help. Avoid want that you help in this meaning.

items.example: I really like the atmosphere in this café.
items.note: Really normally comes before like: I really like it. Avoid I very like it.

items.example: I don't like this colour very much.
items.note: Place very much after the object of like: I do not like it very much. The dots indicate the object.

items.example: 'How is your father?' 'Very well, thanks.'
items.note: A natural reply about health: Very well, thanks. Well refers to health in this context.

items.example: 'How's your aunt?' 'She's better now.'
items.note: How's is short for how is. Add a person to ask about their health or how things are going.

items.example: 'My sister is fine.' 'And how about your brother?'
items.note: Use how about to ask about another person or to change the focus of a conversation.

items.example: We're a bit nervous about the presentation.
items.note: A bit softens an adjective: a bit tired or a bit upset. Keep the article a.

items.example: He felt a little cold on the boat.
items.note: A little can soften an adjective: a little tired. It can also describe a small amount of an uncountable noun.

items.section: Exercises · Productive use and error correction
items.example: I feel happy when I visit the countryside.
items.note: Use feel + adjective to talk about emotions or physical sensations: feel sad, feel cold.

items.section: Exercises · Productive use and error correction
items.example: I like reading on the train.
items.note: Use like + an -ing form for activities you enjoy: like swimming. The pattern is not a single spoken word.

units.title: Unit 08 — Conversations 1: Greetings and wishes
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd edition, Unit 8, printed pages 22–23 (PDF pages 23–24); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)
learningObjectives: Choose greetings for different times of day, especially good morning, good afternoon and good evening.
Respond naturally to How are you? and continue an exchange with And you?
Use expressions for leaving, making polite requests, thanking, apologizing and attracting attention.
Recognize cheers as informal thanks in British English and Bless you as a response to a sneeze.
Choose appropriate greetings and wishes for birthdays, Christmas, New Year, examinations and achievements.
Distinguish Good luck before an event from Well done or Congratulations after success, and avoid Congratulations as a birthday greeting.
Create short natural conversations using the situations presented in exercises 8.1–8.5.

items.example: 'Good morning, Mr Evans. Is the office open?'
items.note: A greeting used in the morning, including when answering the phone professionally.

items.example: 'Good afternoon. I'd like to speak to the manager.'
items.note: A greeting used after midday and before the evening. Exercise 8.3 practises choosing greetings by time.

items.example: 'Good evening, everyone. Thank you for coming.'
items.note: A greeting when meeting someone in the evening. Do not confuse it with goodnight, used when leaving or going to bed.

items.example: 'Hello, Olivia. It's nice to see you.'
items.note: A common greeting in both formal and informal situations.

items.example: 'Hi, Sam! Are you free this afternoon?'
items.note: An informal alternative to hello, especially with people you know.

items.example: 'How are you today?' 'I'm very well, thanks.'
items.note: A conventional greeting asking how someone is; the answer is often short.

items.example: 'How are you?' 'Fine, thanks.'
items.note: A brief, polite reply to How are you?

items.example: 'I'm fine, thanks. And you?'
items.note: Use And you? to return a question to the other speaker without repeating the whole question.

items.example: 'How's everything?' 'Not too bad, thanks.'
items.note: A moderately positive, conversational response to How are you?

items.example: 'Goodbye, Ms Jones. Have a safe trip.'
items.note: A farewell used when leaving, not when arriving.

items.example: 'I have to leave now. See you soon!'
items.note: An informal farewell suggesting that you expect to meet the person again.

items.example: 'Goodnight, Dad. I'll see you tomorrow.'
items.note: Use goodnight when leaving someone in the evening or before going to sleep, not as an arrival greeting.

items.example: 'Sleep well. You've had a long day.'
items.note: A friendly wish to someone who is going to bed.

items.example: 'Could you close the window, please?'
items.note: A polite word commonly used when making requests, often at the end of the sentence.

items.example: 'Thank you for carrying my bag.'
items.note: Use thank you to express gratitude for help, a gift or another kind action.

items.example: 'Here's your change.' 'Cheers!'
items.note: In British English, cheers can mean thank you in informal situations; it has other meanings as well.

items.example: 'Excuse me, could I get past you?'
items.note: Use excuse me to attract attention politely or ask someone to let you pass.

items.example: 'Sorry, I didn't see your bag on the floor.'
items.note: Use sorry when apologizing for a mistake or inconvenience. Compare excuse me before asking to pass.

items.example: 'Achoo!' 'Bless you!'
items.note: A customary response when someone sneezes.

items.example: 'Happy birthday, Leo! I hope you enjoy your day.'
items.note: A birthday greeting. Congratulations is not the usual expression for wishing someone a happy birthday.

items.example: 'Merry Christmas, Alice! See you in January.'
items.note: A common Christmas greeting. Happy Christmas is also used, especially in British English.

items.example: 'Happy Christmas to you and your family!'
items.note: An alternative to Merry Christmas, especially common in British English.

items.example: 'Happy New Year, everyone! Here's to a great year.'
items.note: A seasonal greeting around the beginning of a new year. New Year's Day is 1 January.

items.example: 'Good luck with your interview tomorrow.'
items.note: Say good luck before a test, interview or other challenging event, not after a completed success.

items.example: 'You got the scholarship? Congratulations!'
items.note: Say congratulations after an achievement or other happy event, not as the usual birthday greeting.

items.example: 'You passed the final test. Well done!'
items.note: Use well done to praise someone for a successful action or achievement.

items.example: We're visiting our cousins at Christmas.
items.note: Christmas is a holiday name. The written t is silent: /ˈkrɪsməs/.

items.example: My son's birthday is next Thursday.
items.note: The yearly anniversary of someone’s birth; it is the occasion for saying Happy Birthday.

items.example: Many shops close on New Year's Day.
items.note: New Year's Day is 1 January; the associated greeting is Happy New Year.

items.example: My little brother sneezed twice during the lesson.
items.note: The action of suddenly expelling air through the nose or mouth; someone may reply Bless you.

items.example: 'I passed my exam yesterday.' 'Well done!'
items.note: Pass an exam means succeed in an exam. Use congratulations or well done after someone has passed.
